title: Benchmarking Redis Performance
description: Measure Redis throughput and latency accurately using redis-benchmark and custom load-testing strategies.

data.text: Benchmarking Redis tells you how fast your instance can handle requests before it becomes a bottleneck. The built-in redis-benchmark tool is the standard starting point, but accurate benchmarking requires controlling variables like pipeline depth, command complexity, and network conditions. Without discipline, benchmarks can mislead you into under-provisioning or over-provisioning your Redis infrastructure.

The redis-benchmark tool ships with Redis and simulates N clients sending M requests each. It reports throughput in operations per second and latency in milliseconds. For realistic results, run it from the same network as your application, use pipelining to match your production pattern, and test with your actual key sizes.

data.title: Basic redis-benchmark commands
data.code:
# Run with 50 parallel clients, 100k requests each
redis-benchmark -h localhost -p 6379 \
  -c 50 -n 100000 \
  -t SET,GET \
  --csv

# Pipelined benchmark with depth 10
redis-benchmark -h localhost -p 6379 \
  -c 50 -n 100000 \
  -P 10 \
  -t SET,GET

# With 1KB values to test realistic payloads
echo 'rand:10:1024' | \
  redis-benchmark -h localhost -p 6379 \
  -c 50 -n 50000 -P 5 \
  -t SET,GET

data.text: For application-specific workloads, write a small benchmark harness that mimics your production access pattern. Measure both throughput and latency percentiles — average latency hides tail latency that can affect user experience.

data.title: Essential benchmark metrics
Warm-Up Effect
data.text: Redis performance improves after the first few thousand requests as the kernel buffer cache fills. Always discard the first 5-10 seconds of a benchmark to measure steady-state performance, not cold-start behavior.

items: Running from a different machine than your application, ignoring network latency
Using a single client, which does not reflect concurrency
Testing with tiny keys when your production keys are large
Trusting average latency without looking at P99
Benchmarking an idle instance when your production Redis has background saves

terms.definition: The number of operations completed per second. Higher is better, but only if latency remains acceptable.
The slowest requests, typically measured at P99 or higher. Tail latency often determines user experience more than average.
The number of commands sent in a single network flush. Deeper pipelines increase throughput but also increase response size.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use redis-benchmark for quick baseline checks
Write custom benchmarks to match your real workload
Measure P50, P99, and P99.9, not just average
Warm up the instance before collecting metrics
Profile with MONITOR or slowlog after throughput plateaus
data.takeaway: Benchmarking is not a one-time task. Re-run benchmarks after every infrastructure change, client upgrade, or data-size increase to catch regressions before they hit production.
